title: A Human-Centered Approach to Ethical AI Education in Underresourced Secondary Schools
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how AI education can be designed ethically and equitably for students in under-resourced secondary schools. The authors argue that simple access to AI tools or exposure to AI concepts is insufficient, especially in Title I and Title I-eligible contexts, because such approaches may reproduce inequities and fail to develop students’ ability to reason about fairness, privacy, accountability, and other social consequences of AI. The study asks whether a human-centered course model can support ethical judgment, academic agency, and college-oriented confidence in these settings.

The intervention studied was a college credit-bearing course, Responsible & Ethical AI, offered through a partnership between the University of Notre Dame and the National Education Opportunity Network (NEON). The course used a bichronous model with asynchronous prerecorded instructional content and synchronous discussion-based learning. It emphasized ethical judgment rather than technical mastery, using case analyses, debates, role-plays, reflective writing, and applications of ethical frameworks to real-world AI issues such as bias, privacy, surveillance, automation, and generative AI. Instruction was supported by school-based co-teachers and undergraduate near-peer teaching fellows, with teaching fellows also grading work under faculty supervision.

The population included nearly 180 high school students from 12 Title I and Title I-eligible U.S. high schools, along with 8 co-teachers and 12 teaching fellows. The schools served largely low-income and historically marginalized student populations across multiple states. The paper reports end-of-course survey data from students, co-teachers, and teaching fellows, combining Likert-scale responses and open-ended reflections. Because teaching fellows were undergraduate students serving instructional roles, they are also part of the studied population.

The main conclusions are that students reported strong academic agency, high support and comfort in the learning environment, and especially strong engagement with ethical reasoning about AI tradeoffs. Co-teachers and teaching fellows also described the course as rigorous, meaningful, and supported by the relational structure of mentorship and dialogue. The authors conclude that ethical judgment can be intentionally taught as a core outcome of AI education and that human-centered supports such as mentorship, synchronous discussion, and local classroom facilitation are important equity mechanisms in under-resourced schools. However, the evidence is descriptive rather than causal because it relies on self-reported end-of-course survey data without a control group or pre/post comparison.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods program evaluation using end-of-course self-report surveys and qualitative reflections, with descriptive statistics and triangulation across stakeholder groups. It lacks a control group, pre-post baseline, direct learning measures, and causal identification, so it fits correlational/qualitative evidence rather than rigorous causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings are directionally positive and especially relevant for a priority population—students in Title I and Title I-eligible schools—but impact magnitude is unclear because no causal effect sizes or validated pre-post gains are reported. The evidence suggests promising but not well-quantified impact.

interventions.use_case: Bichronous AI literacy and ethics course delivered through Canvas with prerecorded instructional content, structured assignments, and synchronous discussion sessions for secondary students in Title I and Title I-eligible schools.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the Responsible & Ethical AI course reported strong perceived preparedness for college-level academic work and engagement with course content in AI ethics/civics-type subject matter. Student survey composites showed high academic agency (mean=4.37, SD=0.74) and high judgment-oriented AI engagement (mean=4.65, SD=0.60) on 5-point scales, based on 122 student responses; however, these are self-reported descriptive outcomes without pre-post comparison or causal estimates.
finding.measure: End-of-course student Likert survey composites on academic agency and AI judgment-oriented engagement in a college-credit AI ethics course

finding.finding_summary: The course was associated with positive self-reported durable skill development, especially ethical reasoning, applying learning to new cases, weighing multiple viewpoints, planning, help-seeking, and time management. Students rated AI judgment-oriented engagement highly (mean=4.65, SD=0.60) and academic agency highly (mean=4.37, SD=0.74) on 5-point scales; qualitative responses and educator reports converged that students engaged in sophisticated reasoning about fairness, privacy, accountability, and tradeoffs, though no direct performance-based assessment or causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student end-of-course Likert composites and open-ended reflections; educator perceptions of rigor, discussion, and ethical reasoning
finding.study_size: n=122 students; n=8 co-teachers; n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.60 (AI judgment-oriented engagement); SD=0.74 (academic agency); SD=1.12 (postsecondary trajectory expansion)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported a highly supportive and comfortable learning environment and educators perceived strong engagement and meaningfulness. Student ratings were high for learning support (mean=4.59, SD=0.68) and comfortable learning environment (mean=4.79, SD=0.50), while co-teachers rated perceived student engagement at mean=4.25 and course meaningfulness at mean=4.88; these findings suggest positive effects on engagement, confidence, and belonging, but are based on post-course perceptions only.
finding.measure: End-of-course surveys on learning support, comfort, engagement, and perceived meaningfulness
finding.study_size: n=122 students; n=8 co-teachers; n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.68 (learning support); SD=0.50 (comfortable environment); teacher/fellow SDs reported for some items but not all focal student outcomes

finding.finding_summary: At the implementation level, the course achieved very high completion and was successfully delivered across 12 underresourced U.S. secondary schools through a university-nonprofit partnership model. Nearly 180 students completed the course with a 97.8% completion rate, suggesting feasibility and institutional viability of this human-centered AI education model in Title I and Title I-eligible contexts, though no comparison benchmark was provided.
finding.measure: Program completion rate and stakeholder perceptions of college preparation and postsecondary trajectory expansion
finding.study_size: nearly n=180 course completers; survey subsamples n=122 students, n=8 co-teachers, n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.12 for student postsecondary trajectory expansion; other implementation metrics not reported with SD
